question.title: Complaints
question.text: Humans love to complain to each other. It helps us feel less alone. Think about what happens when a family member or friend is going through a tough time; they call up someone who will listen to their tale of woe. Unfortunately, negative bonding is the default for many groups.
keyPoints: Complaining can function as a form of social bonding by making people feel understood.
Families and work groups may reward negative stories and competitive expressions of hardship.
Group norms can discourage positive comments because members fear exclusion.
People resist abandoning negativity when it provides social comfort and belonging.

question.title: Education Technology
question.text: In 1953 B.F. Skinner visited his daughter's maths class. The Harvard psychologist found every pupil learning the same topic in the same way at the same speed. A few days later he built his first "teaching machine", which let children tackle questions at their own pace. By the mid-1960s similar gizmos were being flogged by door-to-door salesmen.
keyPoints: Educational technology has long promised personalised learning, beginning with Skinner’s teaching machine.
Repeated enthusiasm has faded because effectiveness remains uncertain and traditional teaching structures persist.
Modern software may adapt learning pace but must be guided by sound teaching principles.
Edtech could improve education at scale if it serves pedagogy rather than dictating it.

question.title: Sustainable Development
question.text: The Brundtland Report, Our Common Future (1987), defines sustainable development as "development which meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs". Implicit in this definition is the idea that the old pattern of development could not be sustained. Is this true?
keyPoints: The passage questions the Brundtland definition and assumptions underlying sustainable development.
Predicting future needs overlooks innovation and changing circumstances.
The author challenges static views and assumptions about environmental problems and resource scarcity.
Questioning these assumptions is presented as essential to a better future.

question.title: Prior Knowledge
question.text: What is known as prior knowledge (or pre-existing knowledge) is the knowledge, skill or ability that a learner brings to a new learning encounter. This includes all knowledge that is available before the learning event, and which has been gathered or developed by any means, and in any situation, including both formal and, quite often, informal learning situations.
keyPoints: Prior knowledge comprises skills and understanding learners bring to new learning.
Connecting existing knowledge to new information makes further learning possible.
Teachers activate earlier ideas through introductory review and recall tasks.
Activating mental schemas supports comprehension of new subject matter.

question.title: Compulsory Reburial
question.text: Archaeological human remains can provide evidence about diet, disease, migration and living conditions that is difficult to recover from other material. Rules that require remains to be reburied after a short period can protect cultural and ethical interests, but they can also restrict later scientific study.
keyPoints: Archaeological human remains can provide evidence about diet, disease, migration and living conditions that is difficult to recover from other material.

The difficulty is that research methods continue to improve, so future techniques may answer questions that cannot be investigated with current technology.
Museums and researchers therefore have to balance respect for communities with preservation, education and the long-term value of carefully curated collections.

question.title: Wages, consumption and household debt
question.text: Over the past five years, the wage growth is about five percent, which is very weak. Meanwhile consumption has grown by about fifteen percent, which seems decent. However, housing debt has increased by about forty percent, which is unusual, but can be understandable after the wage and consumption increase. The increase in wages is far from sufficient to cover the increase in consumption. The increase in consumption is not because of the increase in income, but because people are borrowing more money to buy homes. Although people's wages increase, most of the money will go against paying household debt, because people spend a lot of money at home.

question.title: Civilisation as a ship
question.text: Our civilization, which subsumes most of its predecessors, is a great ship steaming at speed into the future. It travels faster, further and more laden than any before. We may not be able to foresee every reef and hazard, but by reading her compass bearing and headway, by understanding her design, her safety record, and the abilities of her crew, we can, I think, plot a wise course between the narrows and bergs looming ahead. And I believe we must do this without delay because there are too many shipwrecks behind us. The vessel we are now aboard is not merely the biggest of all time; it is also the only one left. The future of everything we have accomplished since our intelligence evolved will depend on the wisdom of our actions over the next few years. Like all creatures, humans have made their way in the world so far by trial and error. Unlike other creatures, we have a presence so colossal that error is a luxury we can no longer afford. The world has grown too small to forgive us any big mistakes.
facts: Civilisation is compared with a large, fast-moving ship carrying humanity into the future.
Although hazards cannot all be predicted, understanding the ship, its history and its crew can guide wise decisions.
Past failures make urgent action necessary, and this is the only vessel remaining.
Human influence is now so large that major mistakes from trial and error are no longer affordable.
question.sample: The speaker compares civilisation to a huge ship moving rapidly towards the future. Although not every hazard can be predicted, understanding its direction, design, history and crew can help humanity choose a wiser course. Past failures show why action is urgent. The speaker argues that the future depends on decisions made over the next few years. Human influence has become so extensive that the major mistakes once associated with trial and error can no longer be afforded.

question.name: Summarise Group Discussion
question.instruction: Listen to the three speakers once. Prepare for 10 seconds, then summarise their discussion within two minutes.
question.title: Tackling a college essay
question.narration: Three students are discussing how to tackle the challenge of writing a college essay.
turns: Speaker 1

Guys, I'm really struggling with this essay. It's so much more difficult than high school, and I have no idea where to start. It's just overwhelming. I keep rereading the prompt, but I'm still not sure if I'm interpreting it correctly.
Speaker 2

Hey, don't worry too much about it. The first thing you should do is to make sure you understand the question. Trying to write without a clear idea of what you're supposed to be discussing will just make things harder. Maybe try breaking the prompt down into smaller parts or even talk to your professor after class to clarify what they're looking for.
Speaker 3

Yeah. You don't need to start by writing the summary or introduction. Just start with the main content first. Get all your ideas down, and then you can organize them into a logical order later. I always do a brain dump first just writing everything I know or think about the topic without worrying about structure.
Speaker 2

That's true. Once you have your main points, you can write a draft and then go back and revise. You might find it easier to write the summary once you've done that. And don't forget, we're here to help, too. We can proofread your draft and give you some feedback. If you want, we could even set up a study session this weekend to go over your outline together.
Speaker 1
That sounds like a good plan. I feel much better about this now. I think I'll try the brain dump method tonight and then maybe share my rough points with you tomorrow.
Speaker 3
The writing center on campus is also a great resource. They can help you brainstorm ideas and even review your essay before you submit it.
Speaker 2

Exactly, don't hesitate to use the resources available to you. And take breaks too when you find yourself stuck. Sometimes stepping away for a bit can help clear your mind and give you a fresh perspective. I always set a timer like 45 minutes of writing, then a 10-minute break. It keeps me from burning out.
Speaker 1

Yeah, you guys make a lot of sense. I'll start by understanding the question and then move on from there. And I'll definitely use the writing center's help, too. Thank you so much! I was so stressed earlier, but now I actually have a clear starting point.
Speaker 3

You're welcome! Just remember to take it one step at a time. Writing an essay doesn't have to be a huge, insurmountable task. You're capable of breaking it down and conquering it, piece by piece. And honestly, your first draft doesn't have to be perfect just getting something on paper is already progress.
Speaker 2
Exactly, remember we're only a call away. We all struggle at times, but that's how we learn and grow. You've got this!
facts: The discussion concerns helping a student who feels overwhelmed by a college essay and is unsure about the prompt.
Speaker 2 recommends understanding the question, breaking it into parts or asking the professor for clarification.
Speaker 3 recommends brainstorming or a brain dump before organising the main content; the introduction or summary can wait.
Speaker 2 offers peer proofreading, feedback and a study session, and recommends regular breaks to avoid burnout.
Speaker 3 recommends the campus writing center and reassures the student that an imperfect first draft is progress.
Speaker 1 feels reassured and plans to clarify the question, brainstorm, share ideas and use the writing center.
question.sample: The students discuss how to approach a difficult college essay. The first speaker feels overwhelmed and is unsure how to interpret the prompt. The second recommends breaking down the question or asking the professor for clarification, then drafting and revising with peer feedback. The third suggests getting ideas down before worrying about structure and using the campus writing center. The second also recommends regular breaks to avoid burnout, while the third stresses that an imperfect first draft is still progress. The first speaker accepts this advice and plans to brainstorm, share rough points and seek support. Overall, the discussion moves from anxiety to a manageable writing plan.

question.name: Summarise Group Discussion

question.title: AI tools for academic assignments
question.narration: Three students are debating over the pros and cons of using AI tools for academic assignments, gathered at a cozy corner table in the library lounge.
turns: Speaker 1

I have serious concerns about relying on AI for academic work. Last week, I reviewed a peer's paper that was clearly AI-generated - it sounded polished but completely lacked original thought. What's the point of education if we're not developing our own thinking abilities?
Speaker 2

I completely agree. The bigger issue is academic integrity. My professor just announced that any detected AI-generated content will result in automatic failure. It's becoming impossible to trust what's authentic anymore. Remember how we used to spend hours in the library actually engaging with sources? That struggle is where real learning happens.
Speaker 3

I understand your concerns, but I think you're overlooking the positive aspects. AI tools have been incredibly helpful for overcoming writer's block and organizing my thoughts. The outlining feature alone has saved me hours of frustration. It's not about replacing thinking - it's about enhancing it.
Speaker 1

But that's exactly the problem! When we rely on AI for organization and structure, we're missing out on developing those crucial skills ourselves. I've noticed my analytical abilities have declined since I started using these tools last semester.
Speaker 2

And what about the classroom experience? If everyone comes to class with AI-polished contributions, how do we have genuine discussions? The imperfections and hesitations in our conversations are where the most interesting insights often emerge.
Speaker 3

I see your points, but consider the accessibility benefits. For students with learning differences or those struggling with academic writing, AI tools provide crucial support that might not otherwise be available. It's not about perfect papers - it's about giving everyone a fair chance to express their ideas. These tools can help bridge gaps for neuro diverse students or those writing in a second language, allowing their ideas to be heard more clearly.
Speaker 1

I appreciate that perspective, but I worry we're creating a dependency. What happens when these tools are no longer available? Will we still know how to think for ourselves? We need to ensure we're not sacrificing fundamental skills for short-term convenience, as true intellectual development comes from working through challenges independently.
Speaker 2

That's my concern too. The value of education isn't just in the final product - it's in the struggle to get there. If we shortcut that process with AI, we're missing the most important part of learning.
Speaker 3
I guess we'll have to agree to disagree. I still believe that when used responsibly, AI can be a valuable tool rather than a threat to genuine learning. The key is finding the right balance.
facts: The students debate the benefits and risks of AI tools for academic assignments.
Speaker 1 worries that polished AI work lacks original thought and that relying on AI weakens analytical and organisational skills.
Speaker 1 also warns about dependency and sacrificing independent intellectual development for convenience.
Speaker 2 raises academic integrity, an announced automatic-failure policy and the loss of authentic classroom discussion.
Speaker 2 believes engaging with sources and struggling through the learning process matter more than the final product alone.
Speaker 3 values AI for overcoming writer’s block, organising thoughts and supporting students with learning differences or a second language.
They remain divided: Speaker 3 advocates responsible, balanced use rather than agreeing to reject AI.

question.title: Origin of Species
question.text:
In 1837, at the age of 28, Darwin wrote "Species Change" in one of his notebooks, which was the earliest record of his evolutionary ideas. Prior to this, he had sailed around the world for 5 years on the HMS Beagle, observing numerous signs that species were not fixed in South America, Oceania, and other places. After returning to England, he wrote "Cuidado" (meaning "be careful" in Spanish) in another notebook, realizing that the theory of evolution was a radical and dangerous view, and that there was insufficient evidence to make it public at that time.

Over the next 20 years, Darwin continuously accumulated a vast amount of data and first presented his views to a small circle of scientists. It was not until 1859, when "On the Origin of Species" was published, that his ideas became accessible to the general readership, causing a great sensation. The first edition of 1,250 copies sold out on the day of publication, and the circulation reached 4,250 copies within a year, receiving both praise from the scientific community and fierce criticism from the religious community and conservative forces.

To this day, "On the Origin of Species" remains one of the most important works in human history, and one of the few works that still has scientific value more than 150 years after its publication. Darwin was well aware that his work was only the beginning. He wrote in the book: "In the distant future, I see open fields for far more important research."
keyPoints: Darwin gradually developed and published evolutionary ideas in On the Origin of Species.
Voyage observations challenged fixed species, but the radical theory initially lacked enough evidence for public release.
He collected evidence over two decades before publication in 1859.
The book stirred praise and fierce criticism and remains influential in science.
question.sample: Darwin developed his evolutionary theory after observing evidence of species change during his voyage, but delayed publication while gathering support for his controversial ideas; when On the Origin of Species appeared in 1859, it provoked scientific praise and religious criticism and became an enduring contribution to human knowledge.

question.title: Working Nine to Five (Independent Work)
question.text: Working nine to five for a single employer bears little resemblance to the way a substantial share of the workforce makes a living today. Millions of people assemble various income streams and work independently, rather than in structured payroll jobs. This is hardly a new phenomenon, yet it has never been well measured in official statistics and the resulting data gaps prevent a clear view of a large share of labor-market activity. To better understand the independent workforce and what motivates the people who participate in it, the McKinsey Global Institute surveyed some 8,000 respondents across Europe and the United States. We asked about their income in the past 12 months-encompassing primary work, as well as any other income-generating activities, and about their professional satisfaction and aspirations for work in the future. The resulting report, Independent work: Choice, necessity, and the gig economy, finds that up to 162 million people in Europe and the United States - or 20 to 30 percent of the working-age population - engage in some form of independent work. While demographically diverse, independent workers largely fit into four segments (exhibit): free agents, who actively choose independent work and derive their primary income from it; casual earners, who use independent work for supplemental income and do so by choice; reluctants, who make their primary living from independent work but would prefer traditional jobs; and the financially strapped, who do supplemental independent work out of necessity.
keyPoints: Many people earn through independent work rather than conventional nine-to-five payroll jobs.
Official statistics underestimate this workforce and obscure its motivations and economic contribution.
A McKinsey survey of around 8,000 people in Europe and the United States identified four motivation and income groups.
An estimated 162 million people, or 20–30 percent of working-age people, participate in independent work.
question.sample: Independent work is more widespread than official labour statistics suggest, with a McKinsey survey estimating that up to 162 million people across Europe and the United States earn income independently, either as voluntary primary workers or supplementary earners or as people working independently out of necessity despite preferring traditional employment.

question.title: Studying Old Plays and Theatre Works
question.text: What are the problems and the benefits for high school students of studying plays and other works for theatre that were written centuries ago? Do you agree with it? Use your own experience to discuss it.
keyPoints: Address both the benefits and the problems of studying historical theatre.
Explain how old plays can develop language, cultural understanding or critical thinking.
Explain difficulties such as unfamiliar language or distant social values.
State whether high school students should study these works and support the view with experience.
question.sample:
High school students can benefit from studying plays written centuries ago, although the material should be introduced with suitable guidance. I agree with including historical theatre because it develops more than literary knowledge, but it should not replace exposure to contemporary works.

Old plays give students an opportunity to examine how people in another period understood family, power, justice and social responsibility. Their language and dramatic structure can also improve reading skills, interpretation and confidence in discussing different viewpoints. When students perform a scene, they must understand the characters' motives and communicate meaning through voice and movement. This makes literature more active than simply memorising information.

The main difficulty is that historical works may contain unfamiliar vocabulary, cultural references and attitudes that modern students find confusing or unacceptable. Without explanation, a class may focus on translating difficult sentences instead of considering the ideas. Some learners may also believe that old stories have no connection with their lives. Teachers can address these problems by providing context, comparing the original work with a modern adaptation and inviting students to question outdated assumptions.

In my own experience, discussing an older play became interesting when my class performed selected scenes and compared the characters' choices with situations today. I realised that the setting was distant, but the conflict about responsibility was still understandable. Therefore, historical theatre deserves a place in high school education when it is taught alongside modern voices and connected to students' experiences.

question.passage: There is a general consensus among mainstream anthropologists that humans first emerged in Africa about two million years ago. Since then we have spread throughout the world, successfully adapting to widely differing conditions and to periodic cataclysmic changes in local and global climate. The many separate societies that emerged around the globe differed markedly from each other, and many of these differences persist to this day. As well as the more obvious variations that exist between peoples, such as language, dress and traditions, there are also significant variations in the way societies organise themselves, in their shared conception of morality, and in the ways they interact with their environment. It is debatable whether these differences are merely incidental artifacts arising from patterns of human migration or whether they represent an evolutionary trait that is key to our success as a species. By analogy with biodiversity, which is thought to be essential to the long-term survival of life on earth, it can be argued that cultural diversity may be vital for the long-term survival of humanity, and that the conservation of indigenous cultures may be as important to humankind as the conservation of species and ecosystems is to life in general.

question.title: Museums and community stories
question.text: A museum collection can tell us about the past, but the meaning of an object is not always obvious from its appearance. A simple tool may reveal little until someone explains who used it, how it was made, and why it mattered in everyday life. This is one reason museums increasingly invite communities to contribute stories as well as objects. Personal accounts can connect a collection to experiences that formal records overlook. However, collecting a story creates responsibilities. Contributors should understand how their words will be used, and museums should distinguish personal memories from independently verified facts. Different people may remember the same event in different ways. Presenting these differences carefully can encourage visitors to think about how historical knowledge is constructed. Digital recordings can make stories available to wider audiences, but they also require attention to accessibility and long-term preservation. A recording is of limited value if future visitors cannot open it or understand it. Community participation therefore involves an ongoing relationship. Museums need to combine professional care with respect for contributors, allowing collections to represent a broader range of experiences without abandoning careful interpretation.
question.prompt: Which TWO responsibilities are mentioned for museums collecting personal stories?
choices: Prioritising recordings over long-term accessibility.
Removing all conflicting accounts.
Explaining to contributors how their words will be used.
Treating every memory as an independently verified fact.
Distinguishing memories from verified information.
question.explanation: Contributors should understand how stories will be used, and interpretation should distinguish personal memory from independently verified facts.

question.title: A neighbourhood weather station
question.text: A neighbourhood weather station can provide useful information, but its location affects the measurements. A sensor placed against a warm wall may report a higher temperature than the surrounding air. Volunteers therefore need clear instructions about positioning the equipment and recording any changes nearby. Regular maintenance is equally important. Leaves can block a rain gauge, and a weak battery can interrupt the record. The aim is not simply to collect more numbers, but to produce observations that other people can interpret with confidence.

question.title: Sleep and learning
question.text: Students often think about learning only in terms of the hours spent studying. Yet what happens after a study session also deserves attention. Sleep provides an opportunity for the brain to process and organise recently acquired information. This does not mean that sleeping can replace learning in the first place. Rather, study and rest play complementary roles. A student who stays awake all night may gain extra reading time but struggle to concentrate or retrieve information the following morning. Regular routines can help because the demands of studying are easier to manage when rest is planned instead of treated as leftover time. The quality of the learning session matters too. Trying to recall a concept and correcting mistakes gives the learner useful material to revisit later. Researchers study these relationships using different tasks, so findings from one experiment should not be assumed to apply equally to every person or subject. The practical message is to consider learning as a sequence of preparation, active study and recovery. A timetable that includes sufficient rest can support this sequence more effectively than one that rewards uninterrupted effort alone.

question.title: Reusing water locally
question.text: Cities usually obtain water, use it once and then send it away for treatment. As demand grows, planners are considering whether some water can be used again for suitable purposes. For instance, treated water might irrigate public gardens or serve certain industrial processes, reducing demand for high-quality drinking water. The important distinction is between different uses. Water appropriate for a garden is not automatically suitable for drinking, and treatment must match the intended purpose. Separate pipes, clear labels and routine monitoring can help maintain this distinction. Cost also matters. A recycling system requires energy, equipment and maintenance, so it should be compared with other ways of reducing demand, such as repairing leaks. Public understanding is another part of the decision. People need clear explanations of where reused water goes, how it is treated and who checks the system. Simply announcing that a technology is safe may not answer their practical questions. Water reuse is therefore one option within a wider strategy. Its value depends on local needs, appropriate treatment and dependable management rather than on the assumption that every available technology should be installed.
